source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — koala
facts: Koalas are marsupials, not bears.
Koalas have two opposing digits on each hand to help grip branches.
Two fused toes on a koala's foot act as a grooming tool.
Koalas choose cooler tree trunks to rest against on hot days.
Koalas can tolerate compounds in eucalyptus leaves that many other animals cannot.
Koalas select among eucalyptus varieties rather than treating every leaf as equally edible.
A koala's low-energy leaf diet is one reason it spends so much time resting.
A newborn koala is roughly jellybean-sized but can crawl into its mother's pouch.
Koala joeys ride on their mothers' backs after outgrowing the pouch.
Male koalas mark trees using a scent gland on their chests.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — wombat
facts: A wombat's pouch opens backwards, helping keep dirt out while it digs.
Wombats can block a burrow entrance with their tough backsides.
Southern hairy-nosed wombats may share extensive burrow systems with other wombats.
Despite their heavy build, wombats can sprint at around 40 kilometres per hour.
Wombats obtain much of their water from the plants they eat.
A wombat can take up to two weeks to digest a meal.
Wombat tunnels branch into separate underground sleeping chambers.
Some wombats have furry noses, while the common wombat has a bare nose.
A newborn wombat is tiny and undeveloped, growing for months inside its mother's pouch.
Wombats are marsupials related to koalas, not small bears.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — tasmanian devil
facts: A Tasmanian devil's wide gape can signal uncertainty or fear rather than aggression.
Tasmanian devils can produce a strong odour when stressed.
Tasmanian devils often scream and growl over food without actually fighting.
Tasmanian devils have powerful jaws capable of crushing bones.
Young Tasmanian devils can climb trees more readily than adults.
Baby Tasmanian devils are called imps.
A mother Tasmanian devil can bear many young but has only four teats available.
Tasmanian devils help clean up their surroundings by eating carcasses.
Tasmanian devils may shelter in abandoned wombat burrows.
A contagious facial cancer can spread between Tasmanian devils through biting.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — kangaroo and wallaby
facts: A kangaroo's muscular tail helps it balance and turn during a hop.
Kangaroos can warn one another of danger by thumping their feet.
Kangaroo mothers can call their young with clicking or clucking sounds.
Some kangaroos live in trees instead of bounding across open plains.
Rock wallabies can negotiate remarkably steep rocky terrain.
The name of the kangaroo family means big feet.
Larger kangaroos can cover more than seven metres in a fast hop.
Kangaroo joeys continue nursing in a pouch long after birth.
Tree kangaroos have relatively stronger forelimbs than their ground-dwelling cousins.
Parma wallabies thought extinct were rediscovered among introduced wallabies in New Zealand.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — red panda
facts: Red pandas belong to their own mammal family, not the bear family.
The red panda was scientifically described before the giant panda.
Red pandas can descend tree trunks headfirst.
A red panda can wrap its bushy tail around its face while resting.
Red pandas grip bamboo with a modified wrist bone that acts like an extra thumb.
Hair on a red panda's soles helps with slippery branches and cold ground.
Red pandas mainly eat bamboo despite belonging to the order Carnivora.
Red pandas may stand on their hind legs to defend themselves.
Red panda mothers move cubs between dens by carrying them in their mouths.
Fossil relatives of red pandas once lived in North America.

source_title: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — giant panda
facts: A giant panda's extra thumb is an enlarged wrist bone.
Some giant pandas are brown and white rather than black and white.
Male giant pandas sometimes perform handstands to place scent marks higher on trees.
Giant pandas can identify individuals and reproductive information from scent marks.
A friendly giant panda greeting can sound like a goat's bleat.
Giant panda cubs are born pink and acquire their dark markings later.
A newborn giant panda is only about the size of a stick of butter.
Giant pandas sometimes eat insects or small animals, despite their overwhelmingly bamboo-based diet.
Giant pandas depend on old trees and hollow stumps for suitable den sites.
A female giant panda is receptive to mating for only a few days each year.
